title: The Burke and Wills Expedition
traveller: Robert O'Hara Burke and William John Wills
intro: The Victorian Exploring Expedition, organised by the Royal Society of Victoria, set out from Melbourne under Robert O'Hara Burke with William John Wills as deputy. Its aim was to cross Australia to the Gulf of Carpentaria, a distance of around 3,250 kilometres, through country most of which had not been explored by non-Indigenous people.
ending: Burke and Wills died on or about 30 June 1861 after the depot at Cooper Creek was abandoned hours before they returned to it. Seven men died in all, and John King, who had been cared for by the Yandruwandha, was the only man who crossed the continent with the expedition and came back alive to Melbourne.

stops.text: The nineteen men left Royal Park at about 4pm, watched by around 15,000 spectators, with twenty-three horses, six wagons and twenty-six camels. Four of the men were camel drivers from the Indian subcontinent. One wagon broke down before leaving the park.
stops.quote: The Burke and Wills expedition set off from Royal Park at about 4pm on 20 August 1860, watched by around 15,000 spectators.

stops.text: Heavy rains and bad roads made travel through Victoria slow, and more wagons broke down. The party reached Lancefield on 23 August and set up their fourth camp.
stops.quote: The party arrived at Lancefield on 23 August and set up their fourth camp.

stops.text: The expedition reached Swan Hill, where Charles Gray joined it. Heavy rains and bad roads had made travel through Victoria slow.
stops.quote: The expedition reached Swan Hill on 6 September, where Charles Gray joined the expedition.

stops.text: To lighten the load, the expedition left behind its sugar, lime juice and some guns and ammunition. Burke dismissed several members, among them the foreman Charles Ferguson, citing lack of funds.
stops.quote: They arrived in Balranald on 15 September. There, to lighten the load, the expedition left behind their sugar, lime juice and some of their guns and ammunition. Burke also dismissed several members of the expedition here, including the foreman Charles Ferguson, citing lack of funds.

stops.text: The expedition reached Menindee on the Darling River after two months, having covered 750 km. Burke divided the party here and left on 19 October with seven men, guided by a Paakantyi man named Dick Barkinji, William Wright and another local Aboriginal man.
stops.quote: They reached Menindee on 12 October, having taken two months to travel 750 km (470 mi) from Melbourne

stops.text: Burke's party, using the pathways of the Aboriginal residents they met at the Bulloo, reached Cooper Creek and formed a depot, later moved to Camp 65, where they built a stockade. On 16 December Burke, Wills, King and Gray set off for the Gulf, leaving William Brahe in charge.
stops.quote: At the Bulloo, they encountered around 120 Aboriginal residents and at times used their pathways to make their way to Cooper Creek, which they arrived at on 11 November.

stops.text: Rain made water easy to find, and the Aboriginal people were peaceful. Wills found the Bynoe River salty and tidal. Burke and Wills went on through swamps, where Kukatj men pointed them in the best direction. They may have viewed the Gulf on 11 February, though no document shows it.
stops.quote: Around 2 February 1861, the group formed Camp CXIX (Camp 119) on the banks of the Bynoe River, an arm of the Flinders River delta, which Wills had noticed to be salty and tidal.

stops.text: The monsoon rains had begun and the party was eating portulaca and a python. Burke beat Gray for stealing porridge. Gray, weakened by dysentery, died on 17 April at a place they called Polygonum Swamp, whose location is unknown.
stops.quote: On 25 March on the Burke River (just south of what is now the town of Boulia), Gray was caught stealing skilligolee (a type of watery porridge) and Burke beat him.

stops.text: With the pack animals dwindling and equipment abandoned, the party shot their only horse, Billy, on the Diamantina River. Three camels had already been shot and eaten, and another abandoned.
stops.quote: they shot their only horse, Billy, on 10 April on the Diamantina River, south of what is today the town of Birdsville.

stops.text: Burke, Wills and King found the depot deserted nine hours after Brahe left and dug up the cache. On 23 April they set off for Mount Hopeless. The Yandruwandha gave them fish, padlu, nardoo cakes and shelter. Burke fired over Yandruwandha heads and knocked fish from their hands.
stops.quote: Burke, Wills and King arrived at Camp 65 in the evening of Sunday, 21 April 1861, finding the Cooper Creek depot deserted after Brahe's group had left earlier that day.

stops.text: Alfred Howitt's rescue party reached the Dig Tree. King, found on 15 September, had lived about a month with a Yandruwandha clan, to whom he gave birds. Howitt buried the remains of Burke and Wills and gave the Yandruwandha tomahawks, knives, sugar and flour.
stops.quote: On 8 September, the party reached Cooper Creek, on 11 September the "Dig Tree", and four days later the two Aboriginal members of the party, Sandy and Frank, brought news to Howitt that King had been found, living with the Yandruwandha.

notes: Journey with legs: Melbourne to Menindee, Cooper Creek and the Gulf, the return. Years for 1860 dates are given by the article's opening lines (1860-61) rather than beside each day. Left out: Torowotto, Bulloo, Lake Altiboulka (named only as waypoints, some are rivers or lakes), Mount Hopeless (never reached), Breerily waterhole and Yaenimemgi where Wills and Burke died (no Wikipedia place article named; the deaths are in the ending and the last stop), the Gulf shore itself (article says unsure they reached it). Camp 119 is placed at Normanton because the article's heritage list puts Camp B/CXIX near Normanton; editor to check point. The Cooper Creek depot and later stops use Dig Tree (Camp 65), the depot moved there on 6 December. Boulia and Birdsville are the towns the article names near the sites. Death dates are disputed: the article gives 28 June (Exploration Committee), c. 30 June or 1 July. Sources conflict on where Gray died. Violence by relief expeditions against Aboriginal people (Walker, McKinlay, Landsborough) is in the article but is not part of this route.
